sources.title: Utilising speech-derived biomarkers to detect Alzheimer's disease with BERT-based language models: a machine learning study
Communication Difficulties as a Result of Dementia - PMC
10 Early Signs and Symptoms of Alzheimer's & Dementia
Subtle changes in speech are associated with early signs of ...

indicators.name: Slowed Speech Rate
indicators.description: Speaking at a reduced speed compared to typical conversation.
indicators.in_picture_description: Describes the photo slowly, with drawn‑out words and noticeable lag between ideas.

indicators.name: Increased Pause Frequency
indicators.description: More frequent and longer pauses interrupting the flow of speech.
indicators.in_picture_description: Their description contains gaps like "... a ... garden ..." indicating frequent pauses.

indicators.name: Word‑Finding Difficulty
indicators.description: Trouble retrieving specific nouns, leading to vague or generic terms.
indicators.in_picture_description: Uses "thing" or "object" instead of naming the vase or lamp in the picture.

indicators.name: Repetitive Responses
indicators.description: Repeats questions or phrases within the same description.
indicators.in_picture_description: Says "What is that? What is that?" while trying to identify a chair.

indicators.name: Semantic Impairment
indicators.description: Uses imprecise or incorrect meanings, mixing up object categories.
indicators.in_picture_description: Calls a sofa a "bed" or a cat a "dog" in the scene.

indicators.name: Reduced Verbal Expression
indicators.description: Provides short, fragmented sentences with limited detail.
indicators.in_picture_description: Says only "Man, tree, house" without further description.

indicators.name: Preserved Syntax and Phonology
indicators.description: Grammar remains correct while content is sparse or inaccurate.
indicators.in_picture_description: Produces well‑formed sentences like "The woman stands near the window" but omits key objects.

caveats: These patterns can also occur as part of normal ageing and are not specific to dementia.
Fatigue, stress, or medication side‑effects may produce similar speech changes.
Variations in language proficiency, accent, or dialect can influence these communication features.
Hearing or vision impairments may affect how a person describes visual scenes.
